notes:
Here are the verse-by-verse notes on 1 Samuel 25:1–22, drawn from the sources reached:

---

## v. 1 — The Death of Samuel

**Traditional Reading:**

Samuel’s death represents the end of the period of the judges. Though we have heard little of him since chapter 19, his influence on Israel was immense — he restored the Law of Moses, founded the prophetic schools, and anointed Israel’s first two kings. "All Israel gathered together and lamented him" indicates that even though he was unappreciated during his life (1 Sam 8:1–7), he was honoured in his death. The phrase "and David arose" immediately after "Samuel died" teaches that God’s work never depends on just one man; when one leader falls, God raises up another.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**Burial "in his house at Ramah":** This does not mean literally inside the dwelling but in a garden or court belonging to his house, since burying inside a house would cause ceremonial defilement (cf. Num 19:15). Similarly Manasseh was buried "in his own house" (2 Chron 33:20), explained as "the garden of his own house" (2 Kings 21:18).
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

**"Wilderness of Paran":** The LXX reads "Maon" instead of "Paran," thinking it unlikely David would go so far south from Maon and Carmel. But Paran gave its name to the vast desert region (the modern El Tih), of which the wilderness of Judah and Beersheba were essentially parts. David may have gone there for safety after losing his protector Samuel.
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html)); Precept Austin ([preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary))

Gill adds that David withdrew to the wilderness of Paran on hearing of Samuel’s death, perhaps to mourn, or for greater safety from Saul, this being further south. He notes that David now "dwelt in the tents of Kedar" (Ps 120:5).
— Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html))

---

## vv. 2–3 — Nabal and Abigail Introduced

**Traditional Reading:**

**"A man in Maon whose business was in Carmel":** This Carmel is not Mount Carmel in the north (tribe of Asher) but a town in southern Judah near Maon (Josh 15:55), about 10 miles southeast of Hebron. The man was "very great" — meaning in worldly possessions — owning 3,000 sheep and 1,000 goats.
— Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html)); Precept Austin ([preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary))

**Sheep-shearing:** This was the "harvest time" for a sheep rancher — traditionally a season of feasting and lavish hospitality. It was the right time for David to ask for compensation.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**Nabal means "fool":** It is debated whether this was his given name or a nickname that stuck because of his character — but he certainly lived up to it. He was "harsh and evil in his dealings" (*qasheh* = hard, stiff, stubborn; *raʿ* = evil, bad morally).
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); Precept Austin ([preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary))

**Abigail:** Her name means "my father is joy." She is praised as "a woman of good understanding and beautiful appearance" — the Hebrew phrase for "beautiful appearance" is applied elsewhere only to Rachel (Gen 29:17) and Esther (Esther 2:7), placing her in elite biblical company.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); Precept Austin ([preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary))

**"He was of the house of Caleb"** (or "a Calebite"): Most commentators take this as descent from the great Caleb son of Jephunneh, making Nabal's wickedness worse by contrast with his noble ancestor (who "had a different spirit and followed God fully," Num 14:24). Others note that *kelev* means "dog"; the LXX, Syriac, and Arabic render it "he was a doggish man" (i.e., cynical or canine in disposition).
— Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html)); Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html)); Precept Austin ([preceptaustin.org](https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-25-commentary))

**Typological reading (Gaebelein):** Nabal is a type of the natural man who rejects the Lord's anointed king and the message of peace. His repeated "my bread…my water…my meat…my shearers" echoes the rich fool of Luke 12:16–21 ("my barns…my fruits…my goods"). Abigail typifies the true believer, and when Nabal dies and she marries David, it pictures the believer's death to sin and marriage to Christ (Rom 7:4).
— Gaebelein ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-samuel-25.html))

**Pastoral note on Abigail's marriage:** F.B. Meyer remarked, "It is remarkable how many Abigails get married to Nabals." Alan Redpath added that if such a circumstance has befallen a believer, "that is no reason for you to invoke the law of the country to get out of the entanglement. Perhaps God knew that you needed the fiery trial… The Bible says you must stay as you are."
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)), citing Meyer and Redpath

---

## vv. 4–9 — David’s Polite Request

**Traditional Reading:**

**Why David sent messengers:** David heard Nabal was shearing — a time of plenty — and sent ten young men to greet him politely, not to intimidate. David had protected Nabal’s shepherds and flocks from Philistine raiders and desert marauders. He waited until "harvest time" to request compensation, leaving the amount entirely to Nabal’s generosity ("whatever comes to your hand").
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**Not a "protection racket":** Though it may sound like one to modern ears, David genuinely performed a valuable service and had a right to expect compensation in a culture where sheep-shearing was accompanied by generous hospitality.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

**"Him that liveth in prosperity"** (v. 6): The Hebrew *lechai* is difficult. The Vulgate renders it "to my brother"; the LXX "for times." Most take it as a popular congratulatory expression like Luther’s "glück auf" — "may it turn out well" or "good luck to you."
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

**"We come on a feast day"** (v. 8): David politely appealed to the traditions of generosity associated with sheep-shearing festivities.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**"Your son David"** (v. 8): David humbly styled himself Nabal’s "son," being of the same tribe (Judah) and recognising Nabal as his senior.
— Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html))

---

## vv. 10–12 — Nabal’s Insulting Refusal

**Traditional Reading:**

**"Who is David? Who is the son of Jesse?"** Nabal could not have been ignorant of David’s identity — David was famous throughout Israel (1 Sam 18:5–7). This was deliberate insult: "Who does he think he is?" Calling him "son of Jesse" was the same dismissive label Saul used (1 Sam 20:27, 30–31; 22:13).
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html))

**"Many servants break away from their masters"** (v. 10): Nabal deepened the insult by implying David was a rebellious runaway slave. This was politically charged — Nabal was likely a Saul loyalist who regarded David as a rebel. This explains why David’s response was so furious: it was not merely personal stinginess but a political declaration of deadly hostility.
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html)); Constable as cited in studylight ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-samuel-25.html))

**"My bread…my water…my meat…my shearers"** (v. 11): Nabal’s repeated "my" reveals his grasping, ungenerous heart. Biblical generosity says "all I have belongs to the LORD," not "this is mine."
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**"Water"** is especially notable: water was precious in this arid region. The LXX substitutes "wine," but the mention of water marks the accuracy of the record — Achsah specifically prayed for springs of water in this same district (Josh 15:19).
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

**The messengers' response** (v. 12): They "turned on their heels" — showing displeasure but admirably refraining from rendering railing for railing. Matthew Henry notes that Christ’s servants, when abused, must leave it to Him to plead His own cause (cf. Luke 14:21).
— Matthew Henry (cited via studylight summary)

---

## v. 13 — David Arms 400 Men

**Traditional Reading:**

David’s immediate reaction — "Every man gird on his sword" — is a low moment. He does not respond as the Lord would have him respond to an insult. Jesus commands turning the other cheek (Matt 5:39). David showed remarkable restraint toward Saul (who actually tried to kill him), but failed to show the same kindness toward someone he perceived as an equal or lower. This is often the true measure of character.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**No inquiry of the Lord:** Unlike at Keilah (1 Sam 23:1–5), David consulted neither God nor the ephod before acting. He was out of touch with the Lord, acting in the heat of his spirit. Gaebelein contrasts David’s rage with Christ’s meekness.
— Gaebelein ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-samuel-25.html))

**400 went, 200 stayed:** The 200 stayed with the baggage (supplies and camp equipment). The Targum says they "were left to watch the vessels."
— Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html))

---

## vv. 14–17 — The Servant Reports to Abigail

**Traditional Reading:**

One of Nabal’s young men (likely a shepherd who had been with David’s men in the wilderness) told Abigail everything. He testified that Nabal "reviled" (literally "flew at," like a ravenous bird attacking) David’s messengers, despite David’s men having been "very good to us" — they were not hurt, nothing went missing, and David’s men were "a wall to us both by night and day."
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html))

**"He is such a scoundrel (son of Belial) that one cannot speak to him"** (v. 17): The servant could not appeal directly to Nabal — he was a worthless, lawless man. "Son of Belial" means "son of worthlessness." The servants knew disaster was determined against the whole household and appealed to Abigail to "know and consider what you will do."
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

The servants' glowing testimony of David’s protection, placed in the middle of an episode that is otherwise discreditable to David, carries great weight. It shows the admirable discipline and kindness David maintained over his band of outlaws.
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

---

## vv. 18–20 — Abigail Acts Quickly

**Traditional Reading:**

**"Abigail made haste":** As a woman of good understanding, she knew the urgency. She gathered an impressive supply: 200 loaves, 2 skins of wine, 5 dressed sheep, 5 seahs of roasted grain, 100 clusters of raisins, and 200 cakes of figs. The fact that so much food was on hand highlights Nabal’s wealth and makes his refusal all the worse.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**The quantity:** The LXX changes "five seahs" to "five ephahs," thinking the amount too small for 600 men. But Abigail was acting in haste and providing for David’s immediate party, not the entire force.
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

**"She did not tell her husband"** (v. 19): This raises a moral question debated by commentators. Constable (Dallas Theological Seminary) argues it was proper since she was attempting to save Nabal’s life — if she had told him, he would have forbidden her and been killed. Enduring Word, however, lists this as one of several things Abigail "did wrong," noting that she acted without her husband’s counsel or approval.
— Constable (cited via studylight); Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/))

**"Under cover of the hill"** (v. 20): The Hebrew *sether hahar* means "a hidden part of the mountain" — probably a hollow or ravine between two peaks. Both parties were descending into the ravine when they met face to face.
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

---

## vv. 21–22 — David’s Rash Vow

**Traditional Reading:**

**"In vain I have protected all that belonged to this man":** David’s words here (and v. 22) are a narrative parenthesis — they reveal what David was saying to himself as he marched, his inner justification for the violence he was about to commit. He had the facts right (Nabal had returned evil for good), but not his heart.
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

**"May God do so, and more also, to the enemies of David"** (v. 22): This is an unusual variation of the common imprecation "May God do so to me and more also" (cf. 1 Sam 3:17). Instead of invoking the curse on himself, David substitutes "the enemies of David." Raschi explains: if God’s anger for a broken vow reaches even David’s enemies (who are distantly connected to him), how much more the guilty oath-breaker himself? A superstitious feeling likely lay behind this substitution.
— Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

**"If I leave one male…by morning light":** David intended to massacre every male in Nabal’s household. This was the reaction Nabal’s own servants expected (v. 17). But God called David to a higher standard than the world’s expectations. David’s anger, while understandable given the political insult and the stinginess, was deeply blameable. The Expositor’s Bible notes that David’s rash vow was "not the result of deliberate consideration" but formed "under the influence of excitement — most unlike the solemn and prayerful manner in which the expedition at Keilah had been undertaken."
— Enduring Word ([enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)); The Expositor’s Bible (cited via studylight)

## Denominational and Other Distinctives

- **Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word, David Guzik):** Emphasises the practical life-application and the work of the Holy Spirit in restraining David. The entire episode is framed as "How NOT to Respond to an Insult," stressing that hurt feelings never justify disobedience. Guzik also notes that Abigail "smoothly suggested the positive outcome" by saying "the LORD has held you back," prophetically guiding David toward the right choice. — [enduringword.com](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-25/)

- **Dispensational / Plymouth Brethren (Gaebelein):** Reads the chapter typologically. Nabal is the natural man who rejects the Lord’s anointed; Abigail is the believer (or the Church) who is freed from the old nature (Nabal dies) and married to the true King. Also stresses that David "was out of touch with the Lord" and contrasts his failure with Christ’s perfect meekness. — Gaebelein ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/gab/1-samuel-25.html))

- **Reformed-Baptist (John Gill, 18th c.):** Gill provides meticulous linguistic and historical detail (e.g., Jewish chronology placing Samuel’s death two years before Saul’s; the Targum on "watching the vessels"). He notes that "water" rather than "wine" in v. 11 shows the scarcity of water in the wilderness. No distinct theological divergence from the mainstream traditional reading. — Gill ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-samuel-25.html))

- **Anglican / Broad Protestant (Ellicott, Pulpit Commentary):** Ellicott emphasises that Abigail’s training likely came from "the Ramah schools of Samuel the seer," giving her lofty views of God and honour. He also discusses in an excursus that Abigail’s words in v. 29 ("bound in the bundle of the living") represent an advance in the Old Testament revelation about the afterlife — a point he says modern Christian commentators have missed but Jewish commentators grasped. — Ellicott ([studylight.org](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-25.html))

- **Methodist / Wesleyan and Lutheran pages:** No distinct results were returned within the search limits for this passage from seedbed.com, lcms.org, or 1517.org.
